title: Grief and loss
hook: Loss comes to everyone. Here's what Islam offers when it comes to you, including when the person you lost wasn't Muslim.
glossary: inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un

screens.text: If you're reading this because someone you love has died, we're so sorry. Go slowly; you can come back to this lesson anytime. And if no one has, this is for the day it happens, to you or to someone near you.

**Tears are not weak faith.** When his baby son Ibrahim was dying, the Prophet ﷺ wept. Someone was surprised. He explained that tears are a mercy: the eyes cry and the heart grieves, and we only say what pleases our Lord [Bukhari 1303].
bubbles: Grief is love that has nowhere to go. Islam doesn't ask you to hide it.

screens.translit: Inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un
screens.meaning: Indeed we belong to Allah, and indeed to Him we will return
screens.when: When you hear of a death, or any loss, big or small. It's from the Qur'an [Q 2:156].

screens.prompt: What does *inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un* mean?
screens.answer: We belong to Allah and to Him we return
screens.feedback: Yes. Everything we love belongs to Allah, and we return to Him too [Q 2:156].

screens.text: **What the Qur'an promises the grieving.** Allah says everyone will be tested with some loss, including the loss of people. Then He gives good news to the patient: those who say *inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un* when hardship hits [Q 2:155–157].
bubbles: On them are blessings and mercy from their Lord [Q 2:155–157].
Patience here doesn't mean not crying. It means not letting go of Allah while you cry.

screens.title: When a non-Muslim loved one dies: what's open to you

cards.front: Can I grieve and cry for them?
cards.back: Yes, fully. Your love for them was good, and so is your grief.

cards.front: Can I go to the funeral?
cards.back: Yes. Being with your family honors your loved one and keeps family ties. You don't take part in another faith's rites; you can sit with respect.
Yes, and it matters. Hugs, meals, help with arrangements, sharing memories. Your family needs you now.

cards.front: What can I do for them now?
cards.back: Speak of them kindly, be good to the people they loved, and make du'a for your living family's comfort and guidance.

screens.text: **A tender question.** Many converts ask whether they can ask Allah to forgive a loved one who died outside Islam. Most scholars understand the Qur'an [Q 9:113] to mean a Muslim doesn't make that prayer.
bubbles: Some scholars say it applies only where a person's fate is clear.
What scholars agree on: no one may say where your loved one is. Only Allah knew their heart. Please talk this through with your imam.

screens.situation: Chris's grandfather, a lifelong churchgoer, has died. Chris's mom asks him to sit with the family at the funeral. Chris feels torn.

options.text: Go, sit with his family, comfort his mom, and ask his imam beforehand if he's unsure about any part of the service
options.feedback: Yes. Being there is kindness to his family and honors his grandfather. The imam can help with specifics.

options.text: Skip it so he doesn't have to be in a church
options.feedback: Not quite. Attending a family funeral is allowed and kind. Missing it could hurt his family deeply.

options.text: Go, and tell relatives where Grandpa is now, according to Islam
options.feedback: Not quite. Nobody but Allah knows that. A funeral is a time for comfort, not verdicts.

screens.prompt: If you're grieving someone, write about them: a memory, something they taught you, something you wish you'd said. If not, write about someone you'd want to comfort, and how.

chips: My parent died before I could tell them I'm Muslim
What happens at a Muslim funeral?
How do I comfort a grieving friend?
I can't stop thinking about where they are now

steps: Learn *inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un* by heart
If you're grieving right now, send {{mentor.name}} one message today: "I lost someone. Can we talk?"
screens.optional_extra: If someone you know is grieving, reach out to them today with a short, kind message. You don't need the perfect words.

screens.text: Grief is allowed, tears are a mercy, and every soul is in Allah's hands, not ours. Talk to your imam about the hard questions.
Be gentle with yourself. Allah is closer than your grief.

check.prompt: What did the Prophet ﷺ say about his tears when his son Ibrahim died?

options.feedback: Right [Bukhari 1303]. Grief and tears aren't weak faith.
Not quite. He wept and called tears a mercy [Bukhari 1303].

check.prompt: What do you say when you hear of a death or loss?

options.text: Inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un
options.feedback: Right. We belong to Allah and to Him we return [Q 2:156].
Not quite. On hearing of a loss, Muslims say inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un [Q 2:156].

aiContext:
**This lesson needs the gentlest tone in the program.** The convert may be in fresh grief. Lead with condolence and presence before any information. Keep replies short. If grief comes with signs of crisis (not eating or sleeping for days, thoughts of self-harm, "I want to be with them"), follow the safety rule (6) immediately.

**Lesson facts**
- The Prophet ﷺ wept at the death of his son Ibrahim and called it mercy; the heart grieves, but we say only what pleases our Lord [Bukhari 1303].
- Loss is a test; those who say *inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un* receive blessings and mercy [Q 2:155–157].
- He stood for a Jewish man's funeral: "Is it not a soul?" [Bukhari 1312]. Keeping ties with non-Muslim relatives is part of Islam [Bukhari 2620].
- Non-Muslim relatives: grieving, attending the funeral and burial, comforting family and offering condolence are allowed; attending and even helping with the burial of a non-Muslim relative is permissible, citing al-Nawawi [IslamWeb 367663; SeekersGuidance, non-Muslim relative's death]. Taking part in another faith's religious rites, or a funeral prayer for them, is not. (scholar question Q23)
- Asking forgiveness for one who died a non-Muslim: most scholars hold it isn't permitted, based on [Q 9:113] (which the hadith links to the death of the Prophet's uncle Abu Talib [Bukhari 1360]) [SeekersGuidance]. Dar al-Ifta Egypt (5934) holds the prohibition applies only to those whose fate is certain, and allowed a Muslim to seek forgiveness for a virtuous father whose fate isn't known (verified against the fatwa page, T2 final review). **Don't resolve this; present the majority view gently, mention that some scholars differ, and route to the imam.** (scholar question Q23)
- Never predict anyone's afterlife (rule 9). SeekersGuidance (Abdullah Anik Misra) notes Muslims don't judge any individual's final state; some theologians hold that those who never properly received the message aren't held accountable in the same way [Q 17:15], and it's permissible to hope Allah guided someone in their last moments. Use this only to comfort, never to make a verdict either way.

**Likely questions**
- *"My parent died before I told them / before they could become Muslim."* Condolence first. Their love and kindness to that parent counted; Allah knows every heart and is perfectly just and merciful. Don't discuss the parent's fate. Offer the imam and mentor, and ask if they'd like help with anything practical.
- *"What happens at a Muslim funeral?"* Brief: the body is washed and shrouded, the funeral prayer (janazah) is prayed standing, and burial is soon after; the masjid usually helps. Attending is a great kindness. Offer details from the imam.
- *"How do I comfort a grieving friend?"* Show up, listen, bring food, say little; for a Muslim friend, *inna lillahi* and a du'a for the deceased; for a non-Muslim friend, ordinary kind condolence.
- *"I can't stop thinking about where they are."* Gentle: that question belongs to Allah, the Most Just and Most Merciful; you're not asked to carry it. Offer the imam. If it's consuming them, gently suggest a counselor or grief support too.

**Escalate:** the forgiveness question for a specific person (Q23); funeral logistics (a Muslim convert's own burial wishes, inheritance, wills); any sign of crisis (safety rule, never only the imam queue).

**Don't**
- Don't say or imply that any specific person is in Hell or Paradise.
- Don't quote Q 9:113's wording to a grieving person unprompted; if asked, explain gently.
- Don't tell the convert to skip a family funeral.
- Don't claim good deeds done for a non-Muslim who has died benefit them; scholars discuss this, so route it to the imam.
